newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Norway salmon row goes into rare EU Sunday meeting.
newsitem.headline: Norway salmon row goes into rare EU Sunday meeting.

text.p: The European Commission will make a last-ditch attempt late on Sunday to solve a bitter row over European Union imports of Norwegian salmon which has strained relations between Brussels and Oslo.

The EU executive failed despite three hours of talks on Thursday to agree a proposal by EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan which would have averted the threat of a damaging trade conflict with Norway, which is not a member of the 15-nation bloc.
"It has become a heated issue," a Commission official said.
An extrordinary Commission meeting to decide the issue will be held on Sunday starting at 9 p.m. (1900 GMT).
EU sources said the Commission seemed likely to approve the deal in the end as most members of the EU executive favoured an agreement. The deadline for a decision is on Monday morning.

Brittan's proposal, agreed this week in talks with Norwegian negotiators, was aimed at resolving the fish dispute without the Commission imposing an anti-dumping duty of 13.7 percent on imports of farmed salmon from Norway.

He had earlier considered such an import duty following an internal inquiry accusing the country's producers of receiving state subsidies and dumping the fish on the EU market at less than the cost of production.

Brittan's new proposal includes a minimum price as well as an export tax of three percent on Norwegian salmon, rather than the EU anti-dumping import duty, EU sources said. In addition, Norway had agreed to limit the growth in exports to 10 percent annually over the next five years.
However, EU Fisheries Commissioner Emma Bonino and Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock opposed such an outcome, pressing for stricter conditions.
Kinnock said Brittan's proposal was based on 1996 figures, which he described as a record year for salmon dumping.

He also told reporters it had come at such short notice that there had been no time to discuss it. "Until a couple of days ago we had before us a very thorough Commission analysis which showed strong evidence of dumping conditions," Kinnock said.
EU sources said trade officials may try to negotiate better conditions with Norway in a bid to win the backing of all 20 commissioners on Sunday.
Norway's salmon exports to the EU are worth some 5.5 billion crowns ($778 million) annually. The industry is especially important in rural and vulnerable areas along the coast.
Scottish and Irish competitors say Norway, the world's biggest producer, is flooding the market and depressing prices.
Norway, which like the EU is part of the 18-nation European Economic Area, strongly rejects the allegations, saying Scottish producers have actually increased their market shares.
Norway's share of the market for Atlantic salmon has shrunk to less than 50 percent from 70 percent six years ago.
The trade conflict is seen in Norway as the most serious dispute with the EU since Norwegians rejected membership of the bloc in a 1994 referendum.

Last month, Norwegian Prime Minister Thorbjoern Jagland urged the Commission not to impose the anti-dumping duties, saying in a letter to Commission President Jacques Santer the matter may "lead to most unfortunate complications in the relations between the European Union and Norway".
Most EU countries oppose placing import duties on salmon, but the EU executive has the power to impose provisional duties for six months without the consent of member states.
